extracted.intended_audience: students and educated readers of natural philosophy/physics and social theory (e.g., readers of classical works on motion and sociological analogy)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository chapter on the general principles governing the direction and rhythm of motion, applied across physical, biological, mental, and social phenomena; develops deductions from the persistence of force and gives many illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion follows the line of least resistance / direction of greatest traction
rubrics_metrics.description: Motion of bodies (including organisms and societies) takes place in the direction in which the average of opposing forces is least — equivalently, in direction of greatest traction or the resultant of forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained via composition of forces and parallelogram construction: if resultant is unopposed motion occurs in that resultant's direction. Illustrated across scales: muscular action, migration, emigration, conquest, commerce, choice of industry, road/route selection. Emphasizes that this is a necessary deduction from the persistence of force rather than a mere metaphor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volition and action follow established nervous channels of least resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Volition is an incipient discharge along neural lines previously established by experience; the passing of volition into action completes that discharge, so movements follow lines of least resistance determined by neural pathways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accounts for cases where ignorance or lack of skill leads a person to take a more laborious course: relatively, the coarse he takes is the one presenting fewest difficulties to his present mental state. Experience (own or communicated) establishes channels of nervous communication that make certain courses the path of least resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social movements mirror individual motion and spread toward minimal antagonism
rubrics_metrics.description: As individuals' motions follow lines of least resistance, collective/social changes (population spread, emigration, conquest, internal industry shifts) proceed in directions where the total antagonistic forces are smallest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: early appearance of large societies in tropical fertile regions; settlements on sea-shores; emigration toward countries with fewest obstacles to self-preservation; conquests and migrations as movements into areas with relatively less opposition. The chapter argues these are literal physical processes analogous to individual motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic/social choice minimizes exertion or 'cost' (cost as measure of resistance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual and societal choices of occupation, industry, and exchange arise because they minimize the labour (resistance) required to obtain desired goods; commerce and division of labour arise when producing or procuring by exchange reduces total exertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: selection of agricultural staples according to soil/climate (wheat/oats/rye/maize/rice/potatoes), fishing on sea-shores, mining where coal/ores are abundant; trade begins when production+conveyance labour in an adjacent district is less than local production labour. 'Cost' is explicitly equated with resistance in these economic decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routes, roads, and channels form to minimize total obstructive forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Paths chosen for transport are those combining shortness, levelness, and freedom from obstacles — the ones achievable with the smallest exertion; subsequent improvements (roads, canals, railways) further reduce obstruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed from animal/human trails to macadamized roads, canals, and railways. Notes exceptions where a more expensive route is chosen for time savings because time loss implies loss of force. Includes minor detours (e.g., to avoid a landowner) as still obeying minimization of total obstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion once established tends to continue along the same line (persistence/inertia of motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once motion is set up in a given direction it tends to persist in that direction and becomes itself a cause of subsequent motion along the same line; stopping such motion requires antagonistic forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linked to the mechanical axiom and the persistence of force: moving matter maintains its motion unless acted on. Social analogues: commercial manias, currents of commodities, customs, political agitations continue long after their original cause and require opposing forces to arrest them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural modification by repeated motion reduces future resistance along that line
rubrics_metrics.description: As motion repeatedly traverses a route or medium, it produces structural changes (e.g., river cutting, worn paths, altered tissues) that diminish the matter's obstructive power to subsequent motion in the same direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: river-courses being cut, channels becoming easier for flow; nervous discharge through animal tissue may chemically alter conductivity; in metals conducting power may be transiently decreased by heat generated by electric passage. Emphasizes distinction between motion transformed into other modes (heat) and the structural reduction of resistance that facilitates continued motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm arises wherever antagonist forces are not in equilibrium
rubrics_metrics.description: When opposing forces are not balanced, motion cannot remain uniformly continuous (because relations to sources of force change with movement), so the inevitable alternative to uniformity is rhythm — undulations, oscillations, or periodic movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives extensive natural examples: pennants and sails in wind, leaves and branches, ripples and river meanders, oscillations in machinery, vibrations from collisions, undulations in ether (light, heat), pulsations in aurora and electric discharges. If forces are balanced there is rest (no rhythm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound rhythms result from interaction of multiple periodic forces (beats/interference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple rhythmical forces acting concurrently with differing periodicities produce compound rhythms via periodic coincidence and antagonism — e.g., beats in acoustics, interference patterns in light, fortnightly tide variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and mechanisms: beats from near pitches (sound and silence intervals), light interference causing alternating intensified and diminished light, tides' fortnightly modulation from solar and lunar attractions, sea-surface waves carrying smaller waves of several orders, sand-rill ridges forming and collapsing due to strengthening ripples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent exceptions (e.g., projectile motion) are interrupted parts of larger rhythms
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions commonly described as non-rhythmical (like a projectile's parabola) are in fact portions of much larger periodic paths that are truncated or arrested by interaction with other matter, and their generation produces associated undulations and vibrations in surrounding media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: a cannon-ball's parabolic trajectory (neglecting air resistance) is part of an extremely eccentric ellipse about Earth's centre; explosion and projectile cause atmospheric undulations (whizz, shock) and vibrations in struck bodies. Thus apparent non-rhythmic motions still manifest rhythm in surrounding effects.
